newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African maize industry enters full free market.
newsitem.headline: S.African maize industry enters full free market.

text.p: South Africa's maize industry on Friday strode confidently into a new era of deregulation, looking forward to a season of tougher competition and anticipating fewer disruptions than last year.
Following legislation late last year all controls on the country's maize market, for 60 years swayed by state intervention, officially ended on Thursday with the start of the new season on May 1.
Thursday was the Workers Day public holiday in South Africa.
Traders, producers and farming co-operatives said that the gradual journey to a free market, begun two years back when restrictions on domestic trade were cut first, had smoothed the transition.

Maize prices are now expected to be more in step with world prices, already evident in white and yellow maize futures contracts traded on the South African Futures Exchange (Safex), industry analysts said.

"Because there is no longer any statutory intervention and any interference from a stabilisation fund, the market will operate a great deal better this season," said Hamish McBain, executive director at food and milling group Tiger Oats Ltd.
"I think it will be competitive, but I think things will go smoothly," he added.
Private exporters made their market debut last season but export quantities were limited by the state-owned Maize Board, which also issued compulsory trade permits.

From May 1 these restrictions, along with the board's role as an export agent, which created much confusion and squabbling amongst players last season, fell away. The board, along with other commodity regulatory bodies, is being wound up in the wake of the 1996 Marketing of Agricultural Products Act.
But the grain market is seen little changed from last year.
"We have actually been competing in a free market since last year," Andre Ferreira, an economist at the National Maize Producers Organisation told Reuters.
Agricultural co-operatives, the owners of the bulk of South Africa's grain storage, are expected to retain their position as the country's dominant marketers.

"I don't foresee it will change that we will relinquish the position of being a big player. We do have the infrastructure," said Francois Smit, assistant general manager at Sentraal-Oos, a co-operative which last month converted to a private company.
But competition is expected to be fiercer, especially given a smaller commercial crop this year forecast at around 7.66 million tonnes, well down on last year's 9.694 million tonnes.

"This year we do not have the same export possibilities, the strong international markets and the devaluation of the rand. People are going to have to be much more skilled this year to market successfully," Smit said.
Higher competition is likely to spur proactive behaviour.

"In the past co-operatives sort of sat back and the maize came to them...this season I think we have been first in the market with producers' contracts, even before the farmers have begun to plant," Smit said.
The same holds for exporters: "It was easier last year for exporters to get hold of maize. They just bought it from the board. They now have to make agreements with farmers," a trader said.
Dealings in maize futures on Safex are expected to kick up after a slow start, as the greater uncertainties associated with a free market drive traders to hunt for ways to hedge their risks.
At 0830 GMT on Friday July white maize contracts were bid at 570 rand a tonne and offered at 585 rand. Similar-dated yellow was bid at 560 and being sold at 580.
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
